name: Maya Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Maya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name never goes with your answers. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Seaward Marine, a specialist insurer down by the old harbour that covers boats: fishing trawlers, ferries, a few rich people's yachts. I'm underwriting support, which means I gather everything the underwriter needs to decide whether to insure a boat and for how much: survey reports, crew certificates, past claims. Then I build the file and draft the quote. I grew up around boats, so I like reading about them all day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My family runs a fish wholesale business on the quay; my father buys from the trawlers at five in the morning and sells to restaurants. I use AI tools every day at work to pull the key points out of survey reports, though I still miss things a proper underwriter would catch, like a hull note that changes the price. Mr Lindqvist, the senior underwriter, sends my files back more than I'd like. I married Sami last year; he's an engineer on cargo ships and away two months at a time, and with what we've saved and my share in the family business we've got well over six months covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and nothing more, and that's no bad thing. People got carried away. Good work and good families don't need a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes very little. I'd still use the tools every day to get through survey reports faster. My real challenge is getting good enough that Mr Lindqvist stops sending files back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and take the marine insurance diploma at evening classes next year. I'd build a few AI shortcuts for the team, because I like doing that. And I'd help my father put his invoices on a proper system, because he still does them in a notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a hull note look like, for someone who doesn't know boats?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a line in the survey saying, for example, the steel near the propeller is thinner than it should be. It sounds small, but it's the difference between an ordinary price and a high one. The AI summary sometimes drops a line about thin steel near the propeller, so I read the full survey of the boat myself now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your father does invoices in a notebook. Would he let you change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble for a week. Then he'd tell everyone at the quay it was his idea. That's how most changes happen in my family.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** and nothing more.
**Good work** and good families don't need a revolution.
think: I'd still use the tools **every day** to read surveys faster.
My real challenge is getting good enough that **files stop coming back**.
do: Take the **marine insurance diploma** at evening classes next year.
Build **AI shortcuts** for the underwriting team.
Move her father's **notebook invoices** onto a proper system.

fieldNote: Maya pairs **daily AI use** with traditional values without seeing a conflict.
She has learned to **check AI summaries** after they missed key hull notes.
Her family's **fish business** is already a place where she brings change.

steps.text: Take the marine insurance diploma at evening classes
Build AI shortcuts for reading survey reports for the team
Move her father's notebook invoices onto an invoicing system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, and people should get on with it instead of waiting for the government to protect them. Businesses that use it well will grow, and that creates work. I'd also say young people should learn real skills, not just the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job changes a lot, but I think I'm on the right side of it. Gathering documents and drafting quotes is exactly what AI will take, but someone has to check the AI and talk to the boat owners. I already do half of that with tools, so I'd be the one they move up, if I can get my insurance knowledge up to scratch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Lindqvist to let me run the AI side of underwriting support, and finish the diploma faster. On the side, I'd start offering paperwork help to small fishing boat owners on the quay, safety certificates and insurance forms, using AI to do it quickly. My father knows every skipper, so I'd have customers on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of excitement. I know some people would be hurt by it, and I'd pray for them, but for me it's a door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be hurt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doreen on our team, who's fifty-eight and types every quote by hand. I'd offer to teach her, but I don't think she'd want to learn now. I hope the firm lets her finish out her years with some dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd charge skippers for paperwork help. Wouldn't the AI make that free for them too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In time, maybe. But a skipper back from four days at sea doesn't want to fight a website; skippers want someone they trust to sort the forms. That's what I'd be selling, really: trust and the family name.

say: I'd say it's **progress**, and people shouldn't wait for government to protect them.
Businesses that use it well will **grow and create work**.
think: Gathering documents and **drafting quotes** is exactly what AI will take.
I'm on the **right side** of it, if my insurance knowledge catches up.
do: Ask Mr Lindqvist to let her **run the AI side** of underwriting support.
Offer **paperwork help** to small fishing boat owners on the quay.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, seeing a door opening.
**Sorry** for older colleagues who may be hurt, and prays for them.
S1.quote: A skipper back from four days at sea doesn't want to fight a website; skippers want someone they trust to sort the forms.
fieldNote: Maya sees **opportunity**, not threat, and blames no one.
Her side business sells **trust** and the **family name**, not just paperwork.
She feels for an **older colleague** but believes in markets over protection.

steps.text: Ask Mr Lindqvist to let her run the AI side of underwriting support
Finish the marine insurance diploma a year early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and people will need their families and communities more than ever. I'd say the government should help people retrain, but not pay them to sit at home. And I'd say this is the time to build something of your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My underwriting job is gone by 2028, and so is my little paperwork business, because AI will do that for the skippers directly. What's left for my family is the hands-on side: the quay, the ice, the lorries. That's got about three years until robots come, around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into the family business within the first year and take over everything that isn't fish: buying, sales, scheduling, all done by AI so my father can stay on the quay. I'd put some of my savings into a second refrigerated van, so we can sell further inland. And I'd ask Sami whether he wants to stop going to sea and help with the vans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I've got my family and a plan. It's frightening for about a week, and then you get to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask Sami to stop going to sea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because cargo ships will be among the first to sail themselves once the robots arrive, and I'd rather have him home. We want children in a few years. I'd want him here, not on the other side of the world, when everything shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when robots can handle the hands-on side too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the fish still has to come out of the sea and someone has to own the business. I'd want my family to be the owners of the robots, not the people they replace. That's the most honest plan I've got.

say: I'd say families and **communities** will matter more than ever.
Government should help **retrain**, not pay people to **sit at home**.
think: My job and my **paperwork business** are gone by 2028.
The family's **hands-on side**, quay and lorries, has until about 2031.
do: Move into the **family fish business** and run all non-fish work with AI.
Put savings into a second **refrigerated van**.
Ask Sami to **stop going to sea** and help with the vans.
feel: **Frightened** for about a week, then **ready to work**.
S2.quote: I'd want my family to be the owners of the robots, not the people they replace.
fieldNote: Fast AGI sends Maya home to the **family business**, where she'd run everything with AI.
She **invests rather than saves**, buying a van to sell further inland.
She wants to **own the robots** after 2031, not be replaced by them.

steps.text: Move into the family fish wholesale business within a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough for anyone willing to work. Build skills, build something of your own, and lean on family. I'd say it with some excitement, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My desk job goes around 2030, but I'd have a few good years first. I could grow the paperwork side business and save, then move into the family business properly before the AI arrives. The quay work buys time until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the AI side at Seaward for two or three years and finish the diploma. I'd grow the skipper paperwork business at weekends and put the profits into the family firm. By 2029 I'd move across to the family business full-time and start automating its office side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I'd be busy. Busy is good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say about you automating his office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say he's managed with a notebook for thirty years. Then he'd see the numbers at the end of the month and stop complaining. My father trusts results, not speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Sami's job change your plans in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. With five years, he could keep sailing a while and we'd save his wages. We'd probably have our first child around 2029, once I'm settled in the family business.

Build **something of your own** and lean on family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing. Anyone can learn a new trade in ten years if they put their back into it. I'd be encouraging, at work and in the community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37, with a decade of using these tools under my belt. I think I'd do well out of it. The family business would be stronger by then too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow into a proper underwriter at Seaward, maybe the one who checks the AI's prices on the big ships. I'd keep the skipper business going and slowly modernise the family firm, starting with automatic ordering from the restaurants. Around 2032 I'd decide whether to take over from my father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the family firm to look like by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three vans and orders taken automatically from the restaurants. My father would only do what he loves, which is haggling with skippers at dawn. My brother driving, me running it, and our name still on the side of the vans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people use ten years as an excuse to do nothing. I see it already with some friends. I'd keep nagging them.

Anyone can learn **a new trade** in ten years if they work at it.
think: I'd be **37** with a decade of using these tools.
I'd **do well** out of it, and the family business would be stronger.

S4.quote: My father would only do what he loves, which is haggling with skippers at dawn.
fieldNote: With ten years, Maya expects to **thrive** in insurance and the family firm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, mostly for the people around me who aren't ready, like Doreen, and for Sami at sea. What would help is government money for adults to learn a trade, and fewer rules stopping small family businesses from growing and hiring. Families can do a lot if they're allowed to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about family businesses. Half the harbour quay in my city is family firms, and a family firm can bend when a big company would just cut. That's worth protecting.

headlineQuote: Half the harbour quay in my city is family firms, and a family firm can bend when a big company would just cut.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old underwriting support clerk** at a marine insurer, still missing key survey details.
She uses **AI daily**, married Sami, a ship's engineer, and owns a share of the **family business**.
Traditional and pro-market, she sees AI as a **door**, favouring work and family over handouts.
In every picture her plan runs through **the family firm**, which she would modernise with AI.
Her mood runs from **calm** to **anxious**, never alarmed, thanks to family and savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mostly for unready colleagues like Doreen and her husband at sea.
whatWouldHelp: **Fewer rules** holding back small family businesses.
